questions.stem: You are taking consent from Michael, 38, for laparoscopic appendicectomy for CT-confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis. When you get to alternatives, he asks: "Could I just have antibiotics instead of the operation?" What is the most accurate thing to tell him?
options: No, antibiotics don't treat appendicitis, so an operation is the only option
Yes, antibiotics cure it for good in almost everyone, so surgery is optional
Most settle at first, but about 3 in 10 need the operation within a year
Most settle, and only about 1 in 20 ever need the operation later
questions.why: Antibiotics alone are a real option for uncomplicated appendicitis, but about 3 in 10 patients need appendicectomy within the first year (APPAC 27% at 1 year, CODA 29% by 90 days), and more by 5 years. Surgery is still recommended, and the choice is his.
notes: Antibiotics alone are an evidence-based alternative for uncomplicated appendicitis, so you must offer it as an alternative for valid consent.
Overstates the benefit: around 3 in 10 need surgery within a year and more later, so antibiotics are not a reliable cure.
Understates the failure rate by about six times. Trials show close to 30% go on to appendicectomy within the first year.

questions.stem: It is 18:00. Michael, 38, has CT-confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis diagnosed last night and is now on tomorrow morning's list, about 34 hours after diagnosis. All his observations are in the white zone and only paracetamol is charted. What is the best next step?
options: Call the registrar to flag the delay, ask about tonight's list and start IV antibiotics
Change nothing: he is stable, so wait for the morning list on paracetamol only
Call a rapid response because he may have a perforated appendix with sepsis
Request a repeat CT abdomen tonight to look for perforation before theatre
questions.why: A short delay (up to about 24 hours) is acceptable for uncomplicated appendicitis. Beyond that, flag it to the registrar to get him on tonight's list or first on the morning list, and start empirical IV antibiotics per eTG.
notes: Stable obs do not make an untreated delay of more than 24 hours acceptable. He needs empirical IV antibiotics and the delay escalated.
No yellow or red zone criteria are met, so a rapid response is not triggered. He shows no clinical sign of perforation or sepsis.
Last night's CT already showed uncomplicated appendicitis. With him clinically stable, repeat imaging adds radiation and delay without changing management.

questions.stem: Michael, 38, describes pain that started as a dull, poorly localised ache around his umbilicus and hours later became sharp and settled in the right iliac fossa. What best explains why the early pain was felt around the umbilicus?
options: Somatic fibres from inflamed parietal peritoneum lying over the appendix
Vagal afferents from the appendix projecting directly to the periumbilical skin
Hindgut visceral afferents entering the spinal cord at the L1 segment
Midgut visceral afferents entering the cord at T10, referred to that dermatome
questions.why: Stretch of the appendix (a midgut structure) is carried by visceral afferents travelling with sympathetic fibres to T10, so the pain is referred to the T10 (umbilical) dermatome. It localises to the RIF once the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum is inflamed.
notes: This explains the later, sharp, well-localised RIF pain, not the early vague periumbilical ache.
Visceral pain afferents travel with sympathetic nerves to the spinal cord. The vagus does not supply the skin of the abdominal wall.
The appendix comes from the midgut, not the hindgut. Hindgut pain is referred to the suprapubic region.

questions.stem: During Michael's laparoscopic appendicectomy, the surgeon divides the mesoappendix, which carries the appendicular artery, before dividing the base of the appendix. The appendicular artery is usually a branch of which artery?
questions.why: The appendicular artery comes off the ileocolic artery, the last branch of the superior mesenteric artery. It runs in the free edge of the mesoappendix and is divided or sealed during appendicectomy.
notes: The right colic artery supplies the ascending colon. It does not usually give rise to the appendicular artery.
The middle colic artery supplies the transverse colon and is a long way from the appendix.
The inferior epigastric artery runs in the anterior abdominal wall. It matters for where ports are placed but does not supply the appendix.
